title: Where do you want me to look? Project 0 becomes three scenes
introduction: This week was crit week. On Tuesday Boyd spent the whole class teaching us how to do a crit, and after class he looked at my Project 0 page and gave me one piece of advice that changed the whole project. On Wednesday I rebuilt the page as three scenes. The crit itself is on Thursday, and on Friday the whole class goes to Bristol for the day. The first six minutes of Tuesday’s class were Boyd helping everyone book the train: the 7:18 from Southampton, back the same evening, with Teresa meeting us there. He booked my ticket himself and will email it to me. It is my first trip out of Southampton since I arrived, and I am looking forward to it more than I expected. (Thursday’s crit and the Bristol day will be added to this post afterwards.)
related_work:
Boyd taught us Liz Lerman’s Critical Response Process [1]. It has four steps: first the audience gives statements of meaning (what was strong, what stayed with you), then the artist asks questions, then the audience asks neutral questions, and only at the end are opinions allowed, and only if the artist says yes. The rule that stuck with me is that everyone must speak to every presenter: “better to be wrong than silent”. We practised on Boyd’s AR glasses. I said they looked “cute”, and he asked me what made them cute. I had to point at the blue colour and the style. Pointing at what actually works is harder than it sounds.

Then we practised in pairs. I was with Sam, who is making a small handheld console. I told him it is small and you can really play it, you could take it on the train, and it could replace a board game; but if nobody tells you in advance, it is hard to see what the object is. When he asked about his AI button, I said honestly that my English is not good enough to be sure I understood the answer, and that the info box was big for such a small screen. He said he would update it. Saying something the other person can actually use felt better than just saying “nice”.

The crit is graded half on technique (the code, the choice between sprite sheet and transform, the colours, how it works on different screen sizes, how AI was used) and half on meaning (how the research leads to the story). So I also looked again at my sources. The ending of my page uses one fact from Material Focus: millions of disposable vapes are still thrown in the bin every week in the UK, and their batteries cause more than a thousand fires a year in bin lorries and waste sites [2].
method:
After class I showed Boyd my page. He said the content was fine, but the balance was off: “Equal text, equal image. Where do you want me to look? Make this really big. Right now it is spread out.” He was right. Everything on my page was the same size, so nothing led the eye. This one sentence is the most important thing I got this week.

So I split the one page into three scenes in the same HTML file. Scene one: you take the vape apart and read a fact for each part. Scene two: you meet a person. Six frames tell the story (ten cigarettes a day, quitting, a “healthier” one, the first puff, three thousand puffs a day, can’t stop), one line each, then a button appears. Every press is one puff: the page flips black and white for a moment, smoke comes out, the battery drops, and the mood goes up and then sinks back down on a mood curve. When the battery is empty the person throws the vape away. Scene three: the thrown vapes fall into a heap, and after five of them the heap catches fire. Back and Next buttons in the corners let you move between the scenes in any order.

The second change is colour, and this is where I had to be honest with myself. In the first version I gave every part its own colour just to tell them apart. There was no design thinking behind it; the colours were random. Boyd had said we need artistic consideration, not only function. So now the whole page is black and white, and the fire at the end is the only colour on the page. One thing stands out, which is exactly what he asked for. I kept the colour drawings in a backup folder and made the black-and-white versions with a small script that fills each part black and keeps a one-pixel white outline.

For the character I storyboarded eight actions: holding a pack of cigarettes, throwing the pack, holding a vape, raising it, puffing and smiling, puffing and low, puffing with a flat face, throwing the vape. I used an AI image as a reference for the poses, then traced the main frame pixel by pixel in Piskel (1,314 pixels at 333 × 128) and built the other seven from it, because between frames only the hand, the face and the thing in the hand change. The eight frames go into one sprite strip, two pixels thick, so the character matches the parts, the smoke and the fire, which are all my own pixel drawings.
results_discussion:
The technique is the same as last week, used in new places. Switching scenes is just adding and removing one class: CSS hides every section with display: none, and the one with the class “on” is shown. Back and Next call the same function with the number before or after. The character strip works like the smoke and fire sprite sheets: the background is eight times wider than the box, and one CSS variable, --f, picks the frame; JavaScript only changes that number. The fall of a thrown vape is a CSS transition on transform, like the parts moving apart in scene one. The flash is one line: body.flash { filter: invert(1); }.

Two things were new for me. The mood curve runs on setInterval: every half second the mood sinks a little toward a floor, and that floor gets lower with every puff, so the more you puff the lower you end up. The curve itself is drawn on a canvas with lineTo. And the pile uses createElement: JavaScript makes one new image each time, gives it the class “dead”, and CSS drops it.

I also found a bug that taught me something about order. I added a shortcut so that index.html#pile jumps straight to the last scene. The first time, the scene was empty, because the jump ran at the top of the file before the script had looked up the elements it needed. Moving those two lines to the end of the file fixed it. Scripts run from top to bottom; you cannot use a name before it exists.

My personal practice this week was the tracing itself. Tracing one frame by hand, pixel by pixel, is slow, but it is the only way I really understand how a line turns into a grid, and it is the reason the character does not look like a photo pasted on a pixel page.
conclusion_future_work: The crit is on Thursday. Before that the site has to be on GitHub and linked from this portfolio, and I want to practise saying which research led to which design decision, because that is what the crit asks for. On Friday we all go to Bristol for the day; I will write that part afterwards. The main thing I learned this week is that hierarchy is a design decision, not decoration: one page, three scenes, one thing to look at in each, and the only colour is the ending.
references:
[1] Lerman, L. and Borstel, J. (2003) Liz Lerman’s Critical Response Process. Takoma Park, MD: Dance Exchange. https://lizlerman.com/critical-response-process/

[2] Material Focus (2024) Battery fires in bin lorries and at waste sites reach an all-time high, reported by letsrecycle.com, 13 May 2024. https://www.letsrecycle.com/news/material-focus-reports-71-increase-in-battery-fires-since-2022
